units.title: Major Types of World Climates
units.intro:
Climate is the long-run mix of temperature and rainfall (plus wind, humidity). Weather is today’s sample. Classification in this book is mainly by heat and rain. Vegetation is the living stamp of that pair.

**Why climates sit where they sit:** latitude (sun angle), ITCZ and pressure belts, continent vs sea, ocean currents, altitude, rain-shadow mountains. Eritrea’s plateau is cooler than its latitude because of height — always say both.

cards.title: 1.1 Introduction to Climate
body: Climate is the average condition of temperature and precipitation of a place over a long period of time.
The word climate comes from the Greek klima, which means the inclination of the sun.
Climate is influenced by solar radiation and by the composition of the atmosphere.
Humans, in turn, can affect climate through changing the earth’s surface and releasing pollutants such as carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
The goal of the geographical study of climate is to understand its distribution over the earth’s surface.

cards.title: Expanded notes
body: Tropical wet: high sun every month, convection rain most days, poor soils despite lush trees (nutrients live in the plants). Savanna: ITCZ visits then leaves — a wet season and a fire-dry season. Deserts: Sahara and Arabian sit under subtropical highs; coastal deserts can also sit by cold currents. Mediterranean: dry hot summer, wet winter — west coasts ~30–40°. Polar: low sun angle, albedo of ice.
Humans shift climate locally (city heat, deforestation) and globally (greenhouse gases). That sentence is the bridge to Unit 5 of Grade 11.

cards.title: Write climate as stacked causes
body: **Latitude:** high noon sun all year near the equator; slanted weak sun and long winter nights toward the poles.
**Pressure belts:** rising ITCZ = rain; sinking near 30° = many hot deserts. Winds then carry those air masses onto land.
**Sea vs land:** water changes temperature slowly, so coasts are milder and often wetter on the windward side. Interiors have huge ranges.
**Altitude:** about 6.5 °C cooler per 1000 m. A tropical-latitude plateau can farm like a temperate country. That is the Asmara sentence.
**Currents:** warm current + onshore wind = extra moisture; cold current = foggy coastal desert.
For Eritrea stack them: tropical latitude + Red Sea on the east + plateau height + dry descending or inland air in parts of the west. One-factor answers are too thin.

tips.text: Climate is the average condition of temperature and precipitation of a place over a long period of time. It has profound effects on vegetation and animal life, including humans.
Humans, in turn, can affect climate by changing the earth’s surface and by releasing chemicals such as carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
The main aim of studying climate is to understand its distribution over the earth’s surface.
To understand the diversity of world climate better, the most important aspects must be selected and studied.
Temperature, precipitation and vegetation are widely used as bases for the classification of climate.

The classification of world climates is intended to be used as a useful learning tool. It helps to simplify and organize various types of climates into a system that helps us to understand the distribution and characteristics of each type.

units.title: Soils of the World
units.intro:
Soil is a living mix: weathered rock + organic matter + water + air. Factors (CLORPT style): climate, organisms, relief, parent rock, time. Profile: O / A (topsoil, humus) → B (subsoil, washed-down clays) → C (weathered parent) → rock.

Climate makes soil as much as rock does: hot wet → deep, leached, lateritic; cold → thin, slow; dry → little organic, salty in places. Vegetation both uses and builds the humus layer. Steep slopes keep soil thin (it slides away).

cards.title: 2.1 Understating Soil
body: The process of soil formation is continuous and takes a long time.
The bed rock breaks down and mixes with dead plants and animal remains very slowly.
For example, it takes three hundred years to form one centimeter of soil in tropical areas.
Soils are formed by a process of weathering, which is the disintegration of rocks into smaller particles.

cards.title: 2.3 Components of Soil
body: Soil is made up of a variety of natural components existing together.
Organic Matter: Organic matter generally comprises less than 5% of total volume of the soil.
Inorganic Matter: About half of soil is composed of inorganic matter including clay, silt, and sand.
Clay has properties significantly different from those of larger fragments (silt and sand).
Air: Half of the volume of soil is made up of pore spaces, which provide passageways among soil particles.

cards.title: Expanded notes
body: Good farm soil has crumb structure, dark A horizon, and a mix of sand (drain), silt and clay (hold nutrients). Laterite under rainforest looks red and can bake hard if the forest is stripped. Chernozem / prairie soils are thick and dark — bread-basket soils. Desert soils may be fertile in minerals but lack water and humus.

Texture is the sand–silt–clay mix. Structure is how those grains clump. A clay soil with good crumbs can still drain; the same clay smashed and bare will pond and then bake. pH matters: too acid or too alkaline locks nutrients even if they are present. Farmers add lime or organic matter to nudge pH and structure — not only bags of fertiliser.

On Eritrean slopes the practical sequence is: keep a cover → slow the water (terrace, contour, check dam) → put organic matter back. Wind on bare dry lowlands needs the same cover logic. Soil lost this year is not a next-season crop.

cards.title: 2.5 Soil Profile
body: Soil profile means a vertical cross section of soil from the earth’s surface down into parent material.
Every major type of soil has its own profile.
The most important factor in soil profile is surface water.
If there is no water to infiltrate down through soil, there can be no profile development.

units.title: Population
units.intro:
Population geography asks how many, where, how fast, and how they move. Density = people / area. Distribution is uneven: coasts, river valleys and fertile plateaus are crowded; deserts, high ice and dense forest are thin.

Change = births − deaths ± migration. High birth + falling death (better food/health) → rapid growth (many developing regions in the 20th century). Age-sex pyramid: wide base = young, growing; column = stable; top-heavy = ageing.

cards.title: 3.1 Understanding population
body: The term population refers to the total number of people living in a place or a country or the world as a whole.
The population of Eritrea or Africa or the world, for example, represents the population of these specific places only.
A sub branch of Human Geography called population geography studies population growth, distributions, and densities from their spatial aspects.
The where of people is the basic question to be answered in the study of population in geography.
The study of population is important not only for geographers but it is also vital for humans, as a whole, who live in various regions of the earth’s surface.

cards.title: 3.4 Population Growth and Structure
body: The population growth rate is the rate at which a population is increases or decreases in a given year due to natural increase and net migration, expressed as a percentage of the total population.
The explanation of a population in terms of its age and gender composition is known as population structure.
Age and sex are the most basic characteristics of a population.
A population pyramid is a graphic representation of the percentage or the actual numbers of males and females in different age groups.
In a population structure the numerical measurement of gender distribution in a population is often expressed in terms of sex ratio.

cards.title: How a population changes
body: The demographic story many countries follow: high birth and high death (slow net growth, young deaths) → death rate falls first (health, food) while births stay high (fast growth, wide pyramid) → births later fall if school, city life and women’s options change (narrower base). Migration can hide or exaggerate all of that in one region.

Eritrea’s map of people is a climate map in disguise: the plateau holds more settled farmers; pastoral lowlands hold fewer people but over a huge area; ports are dense dots on a hot strip because of trade, not because the climate is kind. When you write “uneven distribution,” name those three belts.

Urban growth is not only “more births in town.” It is rural push (land shortage, drought, few services) plus urban pull (jobs, school, clinic). Informal housing appears when the built city lags the arrivals — that is a development sentence for Unit 4.

units.title: The Concept of Development
units.intro:
Development is not only GDP. It is whether people live longer, learn, work decently, and keep the environment that feeds them. Indicators: income, literacy, life expectancy, infant mortality, access to water, energy use. HDI-style thinking mixes income + health + school even if the letters HDI are later.

Simple split: more economically developed / less — but it is a line, not two boxes. Development can be uneven inside one country (capital vs periphery). Sustainable development: meet today without wrecking tomorrow’s soil, water and climate (Unit 1–2 coming back).

cards.title: 4.1.1 Causes of Underdevelopment
body: Less developed countries have been trying to improve their economic conditions and they followed various development strategies.
In some countries, income of the population has declined.

cards.title: 4.1.2 Requirements for Development
body: Development is an internal process, and different countries can follow different paths to reach an advanced level.
Every underdeveloped country should identify a long-term stable path that is compatible with its specific conditions.
For development to start as an internal process, certain conditions need to be fulfilled.
Access to resources is one of the fundamental requirements for development.

cards.title: How to argue “developed” on paper
body: Pick three unlike indicators: one money (GNI or GDP per person), one body (life expectancy or infant mortality), one mind (years of school or literacy). Then add one limit: inequality (averages hide a slum next to a tower) or environment (income from mining that strips a slope).

Sectors: a farm country can still be “developing” if most people are in primary work with low yield. Factories (secondary) raise output but need power and skills. Services (tertiary) dominate rich-city job lists. Skipping straight to services without food and power is a shaky ladder.

units.title: The Representation of Relief on Maps
units.intro:
Maps must show height. Methods: spot heights, layer colouring, hill shading, hachures, and **contours** (the one you must master). Contour = line of equal height. Interval is printed on the map — read it before you shout “steep”.

Packed lines = steep. Wide = gentle. Closed loop, values up inward = hill. V pointing up-valley = river valley. Gradient = rise / horizontal distance (same units). Cross-section: tick contours along a line, plot heights, join. Intervisibility: can A see B? Draw the section — a ridge in the way blocks the view.

cards.title: 5.1.1 Physiographic Diagrams
body: Travelers mostly use these types of diagrams to obtain general information about distances, shapes, directions, and sizes of features on maps.
Ancient traveler frequently used these types of diagrams while traveling from place to place.
Nowadays they are mostly used as preliminary information about relief features in the form of simple sketches.

cards.title: 5.1.2 Hachures
body: Hachures are the oldest methods of showing relief.
Hachures indicate the general drainage pattern from top to bottom sections of a slope.
Steep slopes, for example, are represented by heavy and closely drawn hachures.
In gentle slopes, hachures look lighter and also drawn farther apart.

cards.title: 5.1.3 Hill Shading
body: In hill shading technique, steep slopes are shaded more darkly than gentle slopes.

cards.title: 5.1.4 Form Lines
body: Form lines give approximate idea of the area between two contour lines.
Like contours, however, they show the steepness of an area by changing the distances among each other.

cards.title: 5.1.5 Contour Lines
body: Contour lines are the most effective, accurate, and commonest ways of representing heights and slopes of various types of land forms.
Contours are drawn smoothly on the basis of actual field survey.
Contour lines are drawn at regular intervals.
The value of contour lines is mostly written towards the ascending side of a slope.

cards.title: 5.1.6 Others
body: Spot heights represent accurate heights of specific features like mountain peaks, hilltops, bridges, buildings and more,.
Trigonometrical Stations These are points on the earth’s surface that, are used for triangulation survey.
Triangulation survey is a survey in which the area to be surveyed is divided into triangles.
Trignometrical stations are more accurate than the spot heights.

cards.title: Worked habits for map relief
body: Before any calculation: read the scale and the contour interval out loud. Count lines × interval for rise. Measure map distance in cm, multiply by the scale to get ground metres, then rise/run. Leave the answer as a fraction (1 in 20) and as a percent if the paper likes both.

Cross-section: mark A and B, tick every contour the line crosses, transfer ticks to graph paper with a chosen vertical exaggeration (state it — tall spikes are not “real mountains” if you stretched the vertical axis). Join with a smooth line; rivers sit at the V bottoms.

Intervisibility: draw A–B as a straight line on that section. If any land rises through the line, they cannot see each other. Trees and buildings also block, but the mark scheme first wants the landform reason. Spot heights help when a peak sits between two contours.

cards.title: 5.2.1 Even Slope
body: When the rise or fall of the ground remains constant from the bottom to the top of a landform, the slope is called an even slope.
The contour lines, however, are spaced at an equal horizontal distance interval.
In a gentle even slope, for example, the contour lines are spaced wider apart, while in a steep slope, they are close to one another.

cards.title: 5.2.2 Concave Slope
body: The contour lines of this type of a slope are close at the upper part and widely spaced in the lower part.
Since the slope curves inwards one who stands at the top can easily see the bottom of the slope.
In other words, inter-visibility is possible between any two objects standing on the two different heights of a concave slope.

cards.title: 5.2.3 Convex Slope
body: A slope, which bulges or curves outwards, is called a convex slope.
In other words, intervisibility is very difficult in this kind of a slope.

cards.title: 5.2.4 Terraced Slope
body: In a terraced slope, gradient changes several times between the top and the bottom of the mountain.
Pairs of successive contour lines, which rise gently and fall steeply throughout the mountain, represent this type of a slope.

cards.title: 5.2.5 Cliff
body: A cliff is a high and very steep rock or mountain generally facing a sea or a lake.
On a contour map, a sea cliff is identified by very close contours, sometimes merging into one another or even cutting the sea coast.
In overhanging cliff that lies along the coast, much of the lower part has been eroded by sea waves and its upper part overhangs its lower part.
In such cases, the contours representing this kind of landform will cross and cut one another.

cards.title: 5.2.6 Escarpment
body: An escarpment (Scarp) is a comparatively long and regular steep face of a hill, ridge or a plateau.
The erosion of tilted landforms, for example, result in escarpments.
Faulting processes also create escarpments.
The formation of dips is associated with escarpments.
